summary: Choose an explicit dissipation model so released bodies come to rest, and keep engine damping or sleeping distinct from a measured viscous coefficient.
objective: Compare a positive-stiffness oscillator released from rest at nonzero displacement: decaying crossings under damping below critical, or monotonic return at and above critical.
applies_when: A released, struck or stacked body is expected to stop rather than loop forever.
The scene uses a spring, pendulum, pile or rigid-body solver that would otherwise conserve energy.
intent_signals: shock absorber that settles without oscillating
why does the stack keep jittering
example_prompts: Drop a crate onto a floor so it bounces a few times then comes to rest.
Show a car body that returns to ride height after a bump without oscillating forever.
negative_signals: Undamped simple harmonic motion that is meant to continue.
Optical roughness or material shininess treated as friction.
not_for: Undamped oscillators whose period is the subject.
Claims that a renderer material parameter is a damping coefficient.

principles: Distinguish physical dissipation, engine damping and sleeping; they are different state transitions, not interchangeable measured coefficients.
For the comparison use finite m>0, k>0 and b>=0, x measured from equilibrium, x0 nonzero and v0=0. b=0 is undamped; 0<b<2 sqrt(mk) gives decaying oscillations.
For this release-from-rest comparison, critical damping returns without overshoot faster than overdamping. Arbitrary initial velocity can cause a single equilibrium crossing even in those regimes.
implementation: Own displacement, velocity, equilibrium, m,k,b and initial conditions; use the closed form or integrate m x'' + b x' + k x=0 with a declared timestep and tolerance.
If using engine dynamics instead, set damping explicitly and inspect the documented sleep state. Do not map the engine coefficient to b without establishing that mapping.

Wake a sleeping body before an authored impulse. Pause preserves pose, velocity and time. Reset restores the complete initial state, including damping and intended sleep flags; wake a released test body so it can move.
observable_checks: With x0 nonzero and v0=0, the underdamped branch crosses equilibrium and successive peak magnitudes decrease; b=0 has no decay.
At critical and overdamping, this release-from-rest comparison returns monotonically; do not apply that test to arbitrary launch velocities.
For an engine settling scene, declare speed and duration thresholds and inspect clearance independently of sleep. Pause/resume preserves momentum and reset reproduces the initial release.

creative_affordances: Visible shock absorbers, dust puffs or sagging piles can communicate settling without changing the dissipation law.
A side-by-side underdamped versus overdamped pair is a free presentation choice.
known_limits: Rapier damping is documented as a slow-down coefficient, including fake air friction; it is not a measured viscous drag law.
Sleeping stops further simulation of a slow body; it does not certify thermodynamic equilibrium.
Authored reusable guidance; no runtime artifact has been observed for this record.

claims.statement: For the linear viscously damped oscillator m x'' + b x' + k x=0 with m,k>0, positive damping below 2 sqrt(mk) produces oscillations with an exponentially decaying envelope. In a displacement-release comparison from rest, critical damping returns without overshoot faster than overdamping. Zero damping does not decay.
claims.scope: One-degree-of-freedom oscillator with finite positive mass and stiffness; the monotonic/fastest comparison fixes nonzero initial displacement and zero initial velocity. Not a rigid-body contact model.

claims.statement: Rapier applies a linear damping coefficient to linear velocity and an angular damping coefficient to angular velocity, with default 0.0 meaning no damping; a dynamic body that does not move or moves very slowly for a few seconds is marked sleeping and is no longer simulated until woken.
claims.scope: Rapier JavaScript rigid-body API as documented; not a measured fluid-drag law.
